tldr: This study builds an "interaction prior" that embeds hand-object contact dynamics directly into a latent space, achieving highly accurate and natural dexterous manipulation for novel objects and trajectories using only a simple reward.
hero_caption: Overview of PiHand. Faithful tracking experts are trained from mocap data in a physics simulation and distilled into a latent space as an interaction-aware prior capturing hand-object contact. Leveraging this single prior enables efficient transfer to diverse dexterous manipulation tasks, such as tabletop manipulation of unseen objects, object catching, and bimanual handover.
overview:
Generating motions for robot hands or CG characters to manipulate novel objects at will is an exceptionally difficult challenge. Hand-object contacts are discontinuous and prone to slipping, and object geometries vary widely. Prior work has primarily relied on tracking controllers that mimic motion capture (mocap) data inside physics simulators, or on reinforcement learning (RL) using motion priors trained solely on hand movement patterns. However, the former cannot adapt to novel objects or trajectories, while the latter lacks "object contact" in the latent space. Consequently, RL agents must discover contact relationships from scratch through trial and error, severely degrading both learning efficiency and motion naturalness.

To address this, the authors adopted an "interaction-first" insight: why not embed the hand-object interaction itself into the latent space as a prior from the start? The proposed method, "PiHand," consists of three stages. First, physics-based tracking experts are trained on mocap data in simulation to reproduce hand-object motions with extremely high fidelity (Stage I). Next, the behavior of these experts is distilled into a goal-conditioned variational autoencoder (CVAE) that takes only the target object trajectory as input, constructing an "interaction prior" that inherently captures physical contact (Stage II). Finally, when solving novel manipulation tasks, safe and sample-efficient action decisions are made through bounded residual RL exploration within this latent space (Stage III).

In experiments on tabletop manipulation tasks using unseen objects and trajectories from the GRAB and DexYCB datasets, PiHand improved the success rate by nearly 14 to 17 percentage points compared to methods exploring raw action spaces or using hand-only priors. Furthermore, the single prior transferred to dynamic tasks barely present in the training data—such as catching a flying object or bimanual handover—achieving more than 2x to 4x the success rate of the strongest baselines.
contributions: Proposed a novel data-driven physical interaction prior that unifies hand, object, and contact dynamics within a latent space

Developed contact-aware physics expert policies capable of generating high-quality distillation data, achieving a 93.3% tracking success rate that significantly outperforms the prior SOTA (69.6%) in mocap tracking

Demonstrated that a single learned prior enables zero-shot or highly sample-efficient generalization to unseen objects, unseen trajectories, and dynamic tasks (catching and handover) without complex reward engineering or curriculum learning

sections.heading: Why is a "hand-only prior" not enough? An interaction-first approach that integrates contact upfront
sections.summary: When synthesizing dexterous manipulation in physics simulation, conventional mocap tracking lacks generalization, and hand-only motion priors are inefficient because they ignore object contact. This paper introduces PiHand, an interaction-first framework that embeds the hand-object interaction itself into a latent space to overcome these limitations.
sections.details:
Physics-based animation and robot control for dexterously manipulating objects with hands are foundational technologies for VR/AR and robotics. However, contacts between fingertips and objects are subtle and discontinuous, making it difficult to balance natural visual quality with physical correctness.

Existing approaches have largely followed two main streams. One is tracking controllers that follow mocap data in a simulator. While they yield realistic motions, they cannot adapt to unseen objects or trajectories where reference motions do not exist. The other stream relies on reinforcement learning for generative control. However, directly exploring high-dimensional joint spaces (over 100 DoFs for two hands) requires massive trial and error and often leads to unnatural finger distortions. Methods like PULSE and Omnigrasp emerged to learn "hand or body motion priors" beforehand, but they model only human poses and contain no object information. As a result, downstream RL agents must search for contacts in a latent space completely devoid of contact structure, causing dynamic and complex tasks to collapse.

The core idea of PiHand is to "place interaction itself at the foundation of the latent space." It establishes a three-stage pipeline: training physically grounded tracking experts (Stage I), distilling them into a latent representation conditioned on target object trajectories (Stage II), and performing bounded residual exploration within that latent space (Stage III). This achieves high generalization and excellent sample efficiency on novel objects and trajectories without relying on complex curricula or heavily engineered rewards.

sections.heading: From body motion imitation to coupled hand-object modeling
sections.summary: Motion imitation has progressed from single-body human motion (e.g., DeepMimic, AMP) to recent whole-body and dexterous hand tracking. However, generating object manipulation has largely relied on hand-only priors, leaving physical interaction priors that explicitly incorporate contact dynamics an unexplored domain.
sections.details:
The related work for this study is broadly divided into "physics-based motion imitation" and "interaction motion generation."

### Evolution and Limitations of Motion Imitation
Reinforcement learning-based motion imitation has scaled through works like DeepMimic, AMP, and ASE toward diverse whole-body movements and transfer to physical robots. For human-object interaction (HOI) imitation, frameworks like PhysHOI, SkillMimic, and hand-focused systems such as DexTrack and ManipTrans have also emerged. However, their primary objective remains tracking control—accurately tracing a given mocap reference sequence—limiting their generative capability to autonomously synthesize motions in novel scenarios without reference data.

### Motion Generation and the Use of Priors
Meanwhile, leveraging motion priors to solve new tasks has become an active area of exploration. In particular, PULSE introduced a framework that distills whole-body imitation behaviors into a conditioned latent space and explores that latent space during downstream RL. Omnigrasp extended this approach to object grasping, yet the prior itself only captured human motion. Other approaches, such as GraspXL, explore from scratch across large-scale object sets, but discovering subtle contacts in raw exploration spaces requires excessive reward engineering. PiHand inherits the "prior + latent RL" recipe seen in PULSE, but achieves a fundamental breakthrough by replacing the latent space with one where hand, object, and contact dynamics are tightly coupled.

sections.heading: The full PiHand framework: A 3-step pipeline of accurate tracking, latent distillation, and bounded residual exploration
sections.summary: PiHand synthesizes motions across three stages: Stage I trains physics experts that faithfully track mocap; Stage II distills them into a CVAE conditioned on object trajectories; and Stage III solves novel tasks through bounded residual exploration in the latent space.
sections.details:
The overall architecture of PiHand is illustrated in Figure F2, simulating hands (MANO-based, totaling 102 DoFs for both hands) and passive rigid objects in IsaacGym.

### 3.1 Stage I: Physics-Based Hand-Object Interaction Tracking
Mocap data contains only positional coordinates and lacks contact forces and physical consistency. Therefore, expert policies are trained using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) to faithfully reproduce mocap demonstrations in a physics simulator. Because abruptly changing PD control (proportional-derivative feedback control) targets causes fingertip vibration and unstable contact, the policy outputs an increment over the previous correction step and uses a time-integrated residual formulation: $\boldsymbol{Q}_t = \hat{\boldsymbol{q}}_t + \boldsymbol{a}_t$, where $\boldsymbol{a}_t = \boldsymbol{a}_{t-1} + \pi(\boldsymbol{o}_t)$.
The reward design introduces three key techniques: a surface point tracking loss $L^\text{samp}$; a one-sided contact loss $L^\text{cont}$ that penalizes only missing contacts rather than excessive contact to accommodate geometric mocap noise; and an adaptive keypoint loss $L^\text{key}$ that smoothly shifts tracking targets from wrist-local coordinates to object-centric coordinates as the moment of contact approaches. In addition, hard-mining sampling is introduced to focus training on sequences with lower tracking success rates, learning single-hand and bimanual experts per object.

### 3.2 Stage II: Interaction Prior Distillation
The Stage I experts are "privileged" policies that require future hand mocap poses, making them unusable in novel scenarios. To compress this capability into a single generative model, a conditional VAE (CVAE) is employed. The model consists of a prior network $\mathcal{P}(\boldsymbol{z}_t \mid \tilde{\boldsymbol{o}}_t)$ observing only the target object trajectory, a privileged encoder $\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{z}_t \mid \boldsymbol{o}_t)$ with access to future hand poses, and a decoder $\mathcal{D}(\boldsymbol{o}_t^\text{sim}, \boldsymbol{z}_t)$ that generates PD target updates from the current simulator state and the latent variable. Using DAgger-style behavioral cloning loss $\mathcal{L}_\text{BC}$ and KL divergence loss, the encoder is discarded at test time, allowing physically plausible hand motions to be recovered solely from latent variables sampled based on the target object trajectory.

### 3.3 Stage III: Interaction Generation via Bounded Latent Exploration
When tackling a novel object or task, an exploration policy $\pi_\text{explore}$ outputs a latent residual $\Delta\boldsymbol{z}_t$ relative to the frozen prior mean. Crucially, the exploration range must be bounded. Drifting too far from the latent space leads to unnatural, collapsed motions. Therefore, a squashing function using hyperparameter $B$, $\Delta\boldsymbol{z} \leftarrow B\tanh\left(\frac{\|\Delta\boldsymbol{z}\|}{B}\right)\frac{\Delta\boldsymbol{z}}{\|\Delta\boldsymbol{z}\|}$, is applied, enabling stable reinforcement learning while preserving the diversity of the prior.

captions.F2: The overall pipeline of PiHand. In Stage I, highly accurate physics tracking experts are trained from mocap data. In Stage II, they are distilled into a CVAE latent space conditioned on object trajectories. In Stage III, residual RL exploration is performed in the latent space between the frozen prior and decoder to synthesize manipulation motions for novel object trajectories.

sections.heading: From unseen objects to catching a flying apple: Demonstrating overwhelming generalization
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on the GRAB and DexYCB datasets. Stage I experts significantly outperformed prior methods, and Stage III generative policies outperformed baselines by a large margin on novel objects and trajectories. Furthermore, high success rates were achieved on dynamic tasks like catching and bimanual handover.
sections.details:
Simulations were conducted in IsaacGym, with the contact friction coefficient set to a realistic 0.7 (prior works often use 1.0 to 1.5) to avoid making grasps unrealistically easy.

### 4.1 Expert Tracking Performance (Stage I)
On 50 sequences from the GRAB dataset (GRAB50), the method was compared against the representative tracking approach ManipTrans. Under identical conditions, the success rate (SR) reached 93.3% for the proposed method compared to 69.6% for ManipTrans, with a substantial reduction in mean per-joint position error (MPJPE). Even for experts aggregated per-object across the entire GRAB dataset, a high success rate of 84.8% was maintained, confirming that exceptionally clean data can be supplied to downstream distillation.

### 4.2 Tabletop Manipulation of Unseen Objects (Stage III)
Policies were evaluated on the "Tabletop Manipulation" task, featuring initial poses, unseen objects, and unseen trajectories different from training. PiHand was compared against "Action Space Exploration," which searches raw action spaces without a prior, and a "Hand-Only Prior" (equivalent to Omnigrasp) built from hand-only motions.
As shown in Table 2 and Figure F3, the proposed method achieved a 74.0% success rate on unseen GRAB objects, outpacing the strongest baseline (60.0%) by 14.0 percentage points. On unseen DexYCB objects, it recorded a 76.6% success rate, exceeding the baseline (59.7%) by 16.9 percentage points. Most notably, PiHand reached its peak performance in just 900 epochs—roughly 1/10th the training time compared to the 8,900 epochs required by the baseline.

### 4.3 Transfer to Unseen Dynamic Tasks (Catching and Handover)
Adaptability was also verified on dynamic tasks virtually absent from the prior's training data (Figure F5).
- **Object Catching**: Catching an object flying along a parabolic trajectory in mid-air. PiHand achieved 2.0x the success rate of the baseline.
- **Bimanual Handover**: Transferring an object held in the left hand to the right hand in mid-air. Despite extremely demanding contact transitions, PiHand achieved 4.3x the baseline success rate.

### 4.4 Ablation Analysis
Ablations on Stage III components showed that simply executing the prior directly yielded only a 30.8% SR, and adding residuals to decoded actions instead of latent variables dropped the SR to 49.6%. This highlights the decisive advantage of exploring residuals within the latent space. Furthermore, experiments varying the latent residual bound $B$ (Figure F4) revealed that $B=5$ strikes the optimal threshold, preventing latent distribution drift while maintaining high grasp success and natural hand selection (single-hand vs. bimanual diversity).

captions.F3: Qualitative comparison of tabletop manipulation synthesis on unseen objects from GRAB and DexYCB. Raw action space exploration (top row) leads to unnatural finger entanglement, and the hand-only prior (middle row) fails to grasp the object correctly, resulting in failures (shown semi-transparently). In contrast, PiHand (bottom row) lifts objects stably with natural hand poses.
captions.F5: Zero-shot transfer results on novel tasks largely absent from training data. Top row: Catching an object flying along a parabolic trajectory. Bottom row: Mid-air bimanual handover from left hand to right hand. Highly coordinated bimanual motions emerge from a single prior.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: How contact-first priors unlock dexterous manipulation
sections.summary: PiHand dramatically boosts the generation efficiency and generalization of dexterous hand manipulation in physics simulation by using an interaction prior that unifies hands, objects, and contacts. Future directions include extending to articulated objects, whole-body coordination, and real-robot transfer.
sections.details:
With the clear concept of "making hand-object interaction itself the basic unit of the latent space," PiHand simultaneously resolves the long-standing challenges of exploration efficiency and unnatural motion in RL for dexterous manipulation. Its pipeline—refined reward design for mocap tracking experts, CVAE distillation of an interaction prior, and bounded latent exploration—provides a strong foundation for future robotic manipulation research.

At the same time, the authors note several limitations and directions for future work. First, Stage I expert tracking can occasionally fail on extremely rapid motions or sequences with heavy mocap noise, suggesting room for improved curriculum design and data quality. Second, this work focused strictly on rigid bodies; manipulating articulated objects such as scissors or drawers remains an open challenge. Third, because control is limited to the hands, integrating with whole-body locomotion controllers for loco-manipulation is a necessary next step. Finally, since the current setup is confined to IsaacGym simulations using the MANO hand model, retargeting to real multi-fingered robotic hands with different kinematics and achieving sim-to-real transfer represent vital future milestones.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation insights and robustness evaluations supporting stable physical learning
sections.summary: The appendix details cylinder approximation checks to prevent finger self-penetration, the rationale for a lower friction setting (0.7), the grasp collapse mechanism driven by latent residual bound $B$, and robustness evaluations against object mass variations and stricter termination criteria.
sections.details:
Here are key implementation and evaluation details underpinning the paper's strong results.

### Self-Penetration Prevention and Low-Friction Simulation
Because the simulator (IsaacGym) cannot directly evaluate collisions between rigid bodies within the same hand model, finger self-penetration frequently occurs. To prevent this, each finger is approximated by a 1 cm diameter cylinder, and episodes are immediately halted via Early Termination whenever geometric penetration is detected. Additionally, the friction coefficient is intentionally set to a modest 0.7 rather than the 1.0 to 1.5 commonly used in prior work. This eliminates "unnatural adhesive grasps" caused by excessive friction and enforces truly physical, force-closure grasps.

### Robustness to Physical Parameter Variations
In stress tests where object mass was scaled to 4x its nominal value, the hand-only prior suffered a 67.2% drop in success rate, and action space exploration dropped by 52.8%. In contrast, PiHand's drop was limited to just 11.7%. Because its latent space already internalizes contact dynamics-based grasping strategies, it remains remarkably resilient to disturbances.

### Latent Residual Bound $B$ and Grasp Diversity
As shown in Figure F4, when the exploration bound $B$ is set to large values such as 10 or $\infty$, latent variables drift significantly (blue) away from the prior distribution (gray). Under this condition, although the raw success rate increases marginally, the policy defaults to "cradling objects with both hands" for nearly every object, completely losing the human-like diversity of natural single-handed grasps. Constraining the residual to $B=5$ was confirmed to maximize task success while preserving the diversity of the prior.

captions.F4: Analysis of the effect of the latent residual exploration bound $B$. Loosening $B$ excessively ($B=10, \infty$) marginally improves the success rate, but the latent distribution (blue) drifts far from the prior (gray), causing grasping behaviors to collapse into bimanual cradling and destroying diversity. $B=5$ provides the optimal balance.

takeaways: When learning dexterous contact manipulation with RL, using an interaction prior that couples hand, object, and contact dynamics yields vastly superior sample efficiency and generalization compared to hand-only motion priors.

In physics expert training from mocap, a one-sided contact loss that forgives excess contact and an adaptive keypoint loss shifting from wrist-local to object-centric coordinates dramatically improve tracking success.
In latent reinforcement learning using priors, bounding the exploration range of latent variables (Bounded Latent Exploration) is essential to preserve motion diversity and human-like behavior.
limitations: Restricted to rigid bodies, without support for articulated objects such as scissors or pliers.
Controls only the hands from the wrist down (MANO hands), lacking integration with arms or whole-body loco-manipulation.
Evaluations remain strictly in simulation, leaving retargeting and sim-to-real transfer to physical multi-fingered robot hands unverified.
